key_terms.meaning: A model where computing power is bought like electricity: metered per use, no ownership of the plant
A set of homogeneous computers on one LAN, joined by middleware to work as one machine
Many heterogeneous computers across a WAN, pooled to solve one large job, usually across organisations
The master machine in a cluster that accepts jobs, splits them among the worker nodes and collects results
Software sitting between the application and the machines that finds free nodes, sends work and gathers results
The ability to add or remove capacity automatically as load rises and falls
One job split across several processors that all work at the same instant and can share memory directly
Independent computers, sharing no memory, that cooperate only by passing messages over a network
The consumer provisions computing capacity alone, without human contact at the provider, whenever needed
The provider's physical resources are pooled and handed out dynamically so one user never knows which machine serves them
Capacity can be scaled out and scaled in quickly, appearing unlimited to the consumer
Usage is metered automatically, and both sides can see the meter and the bill
Software that hides physical hardware and presents many virtual machines over one physical machine
Infrastructure as a Service: rent virtual machines, storage and networks; you install and manage everything above them
Platform as a Service: rent a runtime, database and tools; you deploy only your code and data
Software as a Service: rent a finished application through a browser; you manage only your own data and users
Two or more distinct deployment models linked by technology that lets data and workloads move between them
Using services from more than one provider at the same time, often for price, features or risk reduction
Service Level Agreement: the full contract between provider and consumer, including the service levels and penalties
The full cost of an option over its life: purchase, power, staff, maintenance and exits, not just the list price
Placing compute and storage near the user or device, so the delay of a round trip to a distant data centre disappears
The rule a mobile app uses to decide whether to run a task on the phone or send it to the cloud

takeaways: Cloud computing is the commercial form of a long habit: pool many computers, share them, and charge each user by the meter.
Clusters, grids and utility computing each solved one piece; the cloud added self-service and billing to make the pool sellable.
Parallel computing shares data cheaply but is limited by one machine; distributed computing spans machines but pays a network cost for every message.
The NIST definition is a test, not a slogan: all five essential characteristics must hold at once.
Every cloud benefit has a matching risk on the other side of the ledger: elasticity brings bill shock, pooling brings shared-fate risk, self-service brings sprawl.
The reference model is the same stack cut at three heights, and the cut point decides what you rent, manage and pay for.
Deployment model answers who owns and who shares the hardware; service model answers what is being sold.
A meter turns usage into money, and the SLA is the contract that says how honestly the meter must behave.
When delay or connectivity is the binding limit, computation walks to the edge or onto a nearby cloudlet instead of a distant data centre.
bank_note: The syllabi stress the definition and essential characteristics, the historical path from cluster and grid to cloud, the reference model with its layers and actors, the three service models, the four deployment models, and SLA/SLO plus economics for the applied questions.

bank.q: Define cloud computing using the standard five-characteristic definition. Explain each essential characteristic and say why all five must hold together.
outline: Quote/paraphrase the standard definition: pooled configurable resources, on-demand network access, self-service, rapid provisioning
On-demand self-service: no human at the provider
Broad network access: standard networks and devices
Resource pooling: multi-tenant, location-independent
Rapid elasticity: scale out and in quickly
Measured service: metering and transparency
Argue why a webmail service without metering, or a hosted server without self-service, fails the test

bank.q: Trace the evolution of cloud computing from cluster computing through grid computing to utility computing. State the limitation each stage removed.
outline: Cluster: homogeneous nodes, one LAN, head node, middleware for job splitting
What a cluster cannot do: scale beyond one site
Grid: heterogeneous, WAN-wide, cross-organisation, virtual organisation
What a grid could not do: easy commercial self-service and one clean bill
Utility: metered, pay-as-you-go, electricity analogy
Cloud adds self-service, elasticity and rapid provisioning on top of utility

bank.q: Compare parallel computing with distributed computing: memory model, communication cost, coupling and typical failure behaviour.
outline: Parallel: shared memory or tightly coupled, all processors act at the same instant, cheap data sharing
Distributed: no shared memory, message passing only, independent machines that may fail independently
Communication: bus/cache versus network, latency and partial failure
Programming difficulty and effect of one node failing
Example of each, then place cloud computing as a distributed system plus a business layer

bank.q: Draw and explain the cloud reference model and architecture. Identify the layer at which IaaS, PaaS and SaaS sit.
outline: Physical layer: nodes, storage, network
Virtualisation layer: hypervisor, VM images, dynamic provisioning
Platform layer: operating system runtimes, middleware, application frameworks
Application layer: the delivered software
Cross-cutting management: provisioning, monitoring, metering
Cross-cutting security: identity, isolation, encryption
Cross-cutting governance and the actor view
Map the three service models to the cut heights

bank.q: Explain the four deployment models and give one Indian use case for each.
outline: Public: provider-owned, shared tenants, common infrastructure
Private: single organisation, owned or hosted, why: control and regulation
Community: shared by organisations with a common concern, e.g. a group of hospitals
Hybrid: two models linked by technology, data and workload portability
Where virtual private cloud fits
One scenario per model with the reason

bank.q: Three customers arrive: a start-up needing raw virtual machines, a firm wanting only to upload code without touching servers, and a small shop wanting mail and accounting without any IT staff. Choose the service model for each and justify by listing who manages what.
outline: Map to IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
For each, draw the responsibility split: application, data, runtime, OS, virtualisation, hardware
Say why the middle choice is wrong for the others
Mention cost shape, control and lock-in for each

bank.q: A workload needs 20 virtual machines for 6 hours every Monday and 2 machines otherwise. Using a meter, an on-demand price and a reserved price, work out a monthly cost comparison and state when reserved capacity loses money.
outline: Compute hourly usage from the pattern
On-demand cost = hours x rate
Reserved cost = fixed upfront or discounted rate
Show the break-even utilisation
State the rule: reserved pays only if steady usage exceeds the break-even
Mention the risk of paying for idle reserved capacity

bank.q: Distinguish an SLA from an SLO. For a service promising 99.9 percent monthly availability, write a sample availability SLO and explain how the provider should report and credit a breach.
outline: SLO: the internal measurable target; SLA: the contract with commitments and consequences
Availability formula: uptime divided by total time, expressed as a percentage
99.9 percent of a 30-day month means about 43 minutes of allowed downtime, stated as a budget
Measurement window, exclusions, reporting, service credits
Why an SLO is normally stricter than the SLA

bank.q: A phone app recognises text in photographs. Using processing time, energy, bandwidth and delay, describe how the offloading decision should be made.
outline: Define the four cost terms for local and remote execution
Local: compute time, battery drain, no network needed
Remote: upload plus server time plus download, bandwidth cost, delay
Decision rule: offload when remote total cost is lower and connectivity exists
Cloudlet and edge node as middle options, with their lower delay
Mention privacy as a rule that can override the cost comparison

bank.q: 'Rapid elasticity is a benefit and a risk at the same time.' Analyse this for a startup that autoscales a consumer app, using measured service and metering.
outline: Benefit side: capacity follows demand, no over-provisioning, launch survives a traffic spike
Risk side: a fault or a loop in autoscaling multiplies instances and the bill
Metering removes the human check on spending
Controls: budget alarms, maximum instance caps, cost per request monitoring
Conclude that elasticity must be paired with governance

bank.q: A hospital chain must keep patient records under strict rules but wants cloud convenience for its appointment site. Evaluate private, community, hybrid and public models and recommend one with justification.
outline: State the constraints: data location, access control, audit, availability
Private: maximum control, high fixed cost, weak elasticity
Community: shared cost with peers under common rules, governance complexity
Hybrid: records in a controlled environment, public-facing site elastic, needs secure linking
Public: cheapest and most elastic, hardest to justify for regulated records
Recommend hybrid or community with conditions, and name the boundary controls

bank.q: The virtualisation layer is what makes multi-tenant pooling possible. Analyse the isolation it must provide and the risks that remain when tenants share one physical host.
outline: How the hypervisor and virtual network create the illusion of a private machine
Shared resources: CPU, cache, network and storage bandwidth as side channels
Noisy-neighbour performance effects
Tenant isolation and segmentation as a control, plus encryption for data at rest
Why pooling is both the source of economies of scale and the source of shared risk
Mitigation list: patching, hardened images, per-tenant keys, monitoring

bank.q: 'Edge computing will replace the cloud.' Evaluate this claim for three applications: video surveillance, train timetable queries and a monthly payroll run.
outline: Define edge computing and its driver: delay, bandwidth, connectivity
Surveillance: local inference wins on bandwidth and delay, cloud kept for storage and training
Timetable queries: cache at the edge, cloud is the source of truth
Payroll: batch, delay-tolerant, cloud is correct
General conclusion: edge and cloud are complementary tiers of one distributed system, not substitutes

glossary.def: A group of similar computers on one local network, joined by middleware to run one job as a single machine.
Pooling many different computers spread over wide-area networks, often owned by different organisations, to work on large shared problems.
Supplying computing as a metered service paid per use, in the way electricity is billed.
Software between the application and the machines that schedules jobs, moves data and hides the hardware layout.
The controlling machine of a cluster that receives work and distributes it to worker nodes.
Running one job on many processors at the same instant, with direct and cheap sharing of data between them.
Coordinating independent computers that share no memory and communicate only by messages over a network.
Automatic, rapid addition or removal of capacity in step with demand.
One physical system serving several customers while keeping each customer's data and work separated.
Using software to create many virtual machines, networks or storages over fewer physical resources.
The program that runs virtual machines and controls their access to the physical hardware.
A service that rents raw compute, storage and network to the consumer, who manages everything above them.
A service that rents a managed runtime and platform tools, on which the consumer deploys only its own code and data.
A service that delivers a complete application to users, usually through a browser, with the provider managing the whole stack.
Cloud infrastructure owned by a provider and shared by many unrelated tenants over the internet.
Cloud infrastructure used by a single organisation, operated by it or by a third party.
Two or more distinct deployment models connected by technology that lets data and workloads move between them.
Cloud infrastructure shared by several organisations that have a common concern such as regulation or mission.
A service level agreement, the contract that fixes the expected service levels, their measurement and the penalties for missing them.
A service level objective, a measurable target such as availability or response time that the provider aims to meet.
The complete lifetime cost of an option, including purchase, power, staff, maintenance and exit.
Cost per unit falling as volume grows, which is why large providers can charge less than small installations cost to run.
Running computation and storage close to users or devices to cut delay and network traffic.
A layer of compute nodes between the cloud and the devices that shares the load locally with lower delay than the cloud.
A small resource-rich node placed near mobile users to run their offloaded work with low delay.
Moving part of a mobile application's computation or data to a remote node to save phone energy or time.
